creator: Jared Bernstein
title: r*!
full_text:
[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!d-zh!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F18e099b3-44e3-4233-876b-68515004a3d7_1124x1122.png]]

Here’s a monetary-policy riddle:

I’m invisible, yet I move.
And yet, as a flit about, I create neither headwind nor tailwind.

Who am I?

r*, of course, aka the “neutral interest rate” aka the rate of interest that neither stimulates nor slows the economy.

Why invisible? Because there’s no definition of the neutral rate, the way there is for unemployment or GDP. As former Fed Chair Powell used to say, “we know it by its works,” by which he meant something quite germane to the current moment: If growth slows and inflation falls, r* is above neutral and vice versa.

Chair Warsh kinda dissed the concept the other day, saying r* is “useful academically” but not something he considers in setting monetary policy.

But I’m not sure he means that. As Claudia Sahm points out, in the same presser when Warsh was pretty dismissive of the concept’s utility in setting monetary policy, he “framed the decision [to hike] as "removing a dose of accommodation" and then distanced himself from the concept [i.e., r*] that defines accommodation.” [That’s why the cute, little ghost is knocking on the Fed’s door!]

Okay, enough with the riddles and throat clearing: here’s whussup with this, from this AMs WSJ (note the subhead re higher neutral rate):

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!VBJf!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8f55ce32-6352-4304-8087-a225365dd501_1368x368.png]]

So, this “academic” issue is catching hold in the mainstream press, which begs at least four questions, the last one being most consequential;

—Has r* gone up?

—If so, how much? What’s its current range?

—Why is it up?

—Why does it matter?

The consensus is that r* has gone up, and not just here in the US. Here’s a simple way to see it, using average US real GDP and real rates over two recent periods.

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Ol3H!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbb4fc97d-aaf6-41b2-bfc7-042cc1fcfaed_950x570.png]]

Growth rates, same. Real rate, higher now. This is what Goldman’s Sven Jari Stehn means when he says in the WSJ piece: “It is a positive sign that the economy can sustain higher rates, because there is essentially more underlying growth.”

How much has it gone up? This recent paper shows an estimate of medium and longer-term versions of r* estimates (in this post, I’m thinking about the medium term, ftr). Taking the average of that medium-term line from ‘22-’26, you get 1.7%, real, or 3.7% nominal (adding on 2% Fed inflation target), which sounds ballpark to me and happens to be where the Fed is now. But an important part of the figure below is the shaded uncertainty intervals, which are largest at the end of the figure, as it’s harder to get a bead on r* in the present (the methods to back it out require lags).

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!QzyS!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2b7ea437-cf37-4e5b-84e1-5847118cd5da_1200x1048.png]]

Why it’s up is the source of endless noodling. I’ve recently written a lot about the sources of rate pressures, citing the shift in AI financing from internal cash flow to debt, the high level of government borrowing (meaning the Treasury and tech bros are competing for debt, pushing up rates), the inflation premium from the war (showing up in higher short-term rates), and a bunch of risk premia relating to current American governance (a polite way to say “bat-crazy president”) and concerns, which I’d say have faded a bit as he’s finding his legs, that the new Fed chair might not quite have the thread.

Note that the first three items on that list are common across advanced economies, helping to explain this:

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!YA5x!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9562f4be-931a-48b3-8ccf-710f8ab7be36_1370x1112.png]]

Why it matters is the big kahuna, as, far from an academic curiosity, r* is an affordability variable. I recently wrote that I’m concerned rates could be higher-for-longer, making life more expensive for regular folks trying to buy a home (higher mortgage rates), borrow to start a biz, buy a car, etc.

That’s all true, but as you see two charts up, r* was higher in the ‘90’s and that was a good economic period for a lot of regular folks, with low unemployment generating solid real median wage and income gains (true, it was also a period of fast-rising inequality).

In this regard, low r* is a sign of “secular stagnation,” meaning more savings than worthwhile investment opportunities. WSJ: “The low rate [was] a canary in a coal mine telling us that the future looks bleak,” said Lukasz Rachel, an economics professor at University College London. “In that sense higher neutral rates is a good news story.”

The problem with that is it’s all macro, and for a while in this country, we’ve had good macro amidst bad micro. This is why I’m skeptical that higher r*—should it persist; if I’m right about “higher-for-longer”—is a “good news story.” The main thing driving secular NON-stagnation is AI, and I’ve got two big issues with AI in this context, and that’s before we get to p(doom), i.e., the likelihood that it’s going to destroy humanity.

One, I worry it’s a bubble,1 and two, even if that’s right, I’m deeply concerned that what economic benefits it generates will flow disproportionately to the top of the wealth scale, which leaves regular folks with higher interest rates amidst stagnant incomes.

Bottom line, a higher neutral rate is an important change, one that is particularly influential in setting monetary policy. But I chose a ghost to represent it because it’s hard to pin down, so while I think it’s up, I can’t be certain. What’s most important, however, is how this impacts the living standards of regular folks, and if higher-for-longer is correct, that’s yet another challenge in the affordability space.

1You might think, if it’s a bubble and it pops, won’t that lower r*? Maybe, but bubble or not, if AI significantly boosts growth, r* will remain elevated (many bubbly technologies had that impact, including electricity, railroads, the internet). Under that scenario, our fiscal outlook improves, btw, so many forces in play here.

notes.note: r* is another name for the neutral rate, the rate at which monetary policy is neither contractionary nor expansionary. It is the Fed's policy rate that can be set above neutral to cool the economy or below neutral to stimulate it.

sources.quote: The neutral rate of interest (also called the long-run equilibrium interest rate, the natural rate and, to insiders, r-star or r*) is the short-term interest rate that would prevail when the economy is at full employment and stable inflation: the rate at which monetary policy is neither contractionary nor expansionary.
sources.explanation: Shows r* is another name for the neutral rate and gives the neither contractionary nor expansionary definition.

sources.quote: The Fed may temporarily set the benchmark federal funds rate, the rate at which banks borrow from each other overnight, above the neutral rate to cool the economy or below the neutral rate to stimulate it.
sources.explanation: Shows the Fed's policy rate can be set above neutral to cool or below neutral to stimulate.
